title: One Land, Two Nationalisms: Islamism v. Zionism
author: M. Reza Behnam
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Guernica_on_West_Bank_wall-680x453.jpg)

Photograph Source: Travel 2 Palestine - [CC BY
2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)

For decades, the political landscape of the Middle East has been shaped by a
momentous ideological collision. On one side stands Zionism; and on the other,
Islamic political activism, Islamism.

Zionism, an ethno-nationalist project that materialized through the
establishment of Israel in 1948, has continued to expand its physical
footprint through militarism, territorial expansion, forced displacement and
Western backing.

Islamism, a 20th century political/religious phenomenon, emerged as secular
Arab governments, Gulf monarchs and international organizations failed to
secure justice for the indigenous populations of the Middle East, particularly
the Palestinians.

By wedding absolute moral conviction to disciplined organizational structures,
Islamism manifested as the primary ideological force standing in direct
opposition to the hegemonic objectives of Zionism.

It should be noted that a majority of Islamists—a designation that often leads
to media stereotyping —[reject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamism) as
blasphemous groups such as ISIS (Islamic State of Iraq and Syria), ISIL
(Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant), or as it is often called in the Arab
world, _Daesh_.

Until the 1979 Iranian Revolution and the establishment of the Islamic
Republic of Iran, Islamism had limited impact. Since then, it has become the
most powerful ideological force across the Muslim world. Islamist movements
have provided the structural organization for resistance; and its
uncompromising political ideology has enabled and provided a counter against
Zionism and Western imperialism.

Perhaps Israel’s most consequential, yet rarely acknowledged impact on the
region, has been its role in accelerating the death of secular politics and
the rise of militant Islam.

To understand why Islamism has ascended as the primary vehicle of resistance,
it is important to revisit the geopolitical architecture of the post-colonial
Middle East, and to recognize Israel’s crucial role in inflaming the fracture
and militancy that defines the region today.

For a short-lived period (1945-1970), the geopolitical horizons of the Arab
world looked radically different.

Led by Egyptian President Gamal Abdul Nasser (1954-1970), the era was
distinguished by modernization, socialist reforms and the bold language of
pan-Arab nationalism and the promise to liberate Palestine.

After decades of internal corruption and authoritarian governance, the dream
of sovereign nation-states—built on shared linguistic and cultural
identity—collapsed following the decisive and humiliating defeat of the Arab
armies in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War.

The collective consciousness and confidence of the Arab world was further
eroded as its leaders struck compromises and signed unilateral peace
agreements with Israel; as Egypt did in 1979 and Jordan in 1994.

An ideological void emerged, as Arab states prioritized regime survival over
confrontation. For populations suffering and witnessing regional devastation,
these state-led efforts at normalization were viewed as capitulation.

The loss of faith in the ideology of secular nationalism cleared the way for
the genesis of a national political identity based in faith. Islamism
presented a worldview entirely independent of Western-drawn borders, post-
colonial state loyalties and Western ideology.

These movements offered a vision that secular regimes found difficult to
counter. By shifting the paradigm from secular nationalism to religious
jihad—armed struggle in defense of the Muslim community (the _ummah_)—Islamism
provided a new framework for mobilization. It also turned the ongoing
frustration and disappointment over Palestinian dispossession and military
humiliations into fuel for transnational unity.

The mantle of external struggle fell to non-state Islamist groups such as
Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and Lebanon’s Hezbollah, supported in their
resistance to U.S.-Israel hegemony by the revolutionary government of Iran.

Political theorists and proponents argue that Islamism possesses unique
structural advantages that make it, unlike secular nationalism, formidable in
confronting Zionism; most notably:

> \+ Transcendence of artificial borders: Islamism derives its influence from
> its trans-national identity with the _ummah_ , rising above the divisive
> borders carved by European colonialism. Regional Arab states, on the other
> hand, have been constrained by economic involvement and military dependence
> on the U.S. and the West, as well as fragile domestic coalitions.
>
> \+ The power of ideological resilience: Secular militant movements can be
> degraded through conventional warfare, elite cooptation, or political
> compromise. In contrast, Islamist movements exhibit a high degree of
> resolution and organizational resilience, which is in large part due to
> their shared theological belief in divine justice, martyrdom and moral duty.
> To a believer, the struggle against territorial dispossession is a sacred
> obligation, not merely a political grievance; making resoluteness a core
> doctrine.
>
> \+ Moral and popular legitimacy: In addition to political resistance,
> Islamist movements also frequently act as community anchors, providing
> needed social services. Because of the help they provide to populations
> alienated by repressive or indifferent central governments, these groups
> build strong grassroots support that protects them from state military
> annihilation.

Ultimately, the conflict between Islamism and Zionism is a struggle between
two deeply rooted and complete belief systems. Zionism seeks absolute control
through exclusive ethno-religious dominance over Palestinian land. Islamism
counters with a vision that totally rejects the legitimacy of that supremacy,
utilizing faith as both armor and weapon.

Amid a landscape of autocratic regimes, failing international laws and failed
secular diplomacy that has yielded decades of suffering and territorial loss,
Islamism offers its followers an unyielding defense against the systematic
erasure of Palestinians and loss of regional sovereignty.

American militarists and their Zionist allies have tried to carve out and
secure footholds across the Middle East through armed conquest and genocide.
In this jockeying, nations and borders have been treated as pieces on a
chessboard, with heavy focus on territorial dominance and force to guarantee
servitude to the West.

In stark contrast, Islamist groups do not rule over territory or maintain
exclusive control over national governments. Their regional strength and
endurance has been won through ideological resonance.

Islamists operate on an ideological and grassroots level, aiming directly at
the spiritual, aspirational and social core of the populous. In a community
exhausted by foreign aggression and domination, Islamism has offered believers
a compelling indigenous narrative of identity, belonging and justice.
